abstract: Veterinary diclofenac devastated three South Asian Gyps vultures, but the basis of their sensitivity is unclear. A stop codon reported in a Cape vulture P450 gene, described as CYP2C19 in a retained intron, was re-examined with public data: 45 genome assemblies, raw reads of seven Gyps birds and a liver transcriptome. The gene is the bird CYP2C45, without a one-to-one human orthologue. The stop (codon 338, CGA[->]TGA) lies in coding exon 7; the intron is spliced normally, the mRNA carries the stop, and the truncated protein lacks the haem-binding cysteine. The stop was found in all eight living Gyps species, homozygous wherever testable, and in none of 27 other raptors, including two killed by diclofenac. It arose once, 1.5-10.6 million years ago on the Gyps stem, and the gene has since evolved near-neutrally. This genus-wide loss marks Gyps vulnerability but cannot explain diclofenac deaths in other raptors.
